extracted.intended_audience: comedy critics, reviewers, and Vulture readers interested in standards for evaluating comedy
extracted.subtask_description: A working rubric for evaluating comedy across formats (stand-up specials, sitcom episodes, sketches), synthesizing recurring evaluative criteria used by Vulture critics. It’s aimed at guiding critical judgment about voice, structure, joke density, risk, and other craft and evaluative concerns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Voice
rubrics_metrics.description: Does this comic sound like nobody else? (Is the performer distinguishable.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Vulture asks whether voice is distinguishable in 30 seconds; used primarily for stand-up specials but relevant for any performer-centered work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Density (laughs per minute)
rubrics_metrics.description: Are there enough laughs per minute to justify the runtime?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For stand-up specials, consider whether laughs per minute are high enough to sustain the hour; analogous concerns for sitcoms (see joke density per page) — density is a quantitative/audible measure of payoff versus runtime.

rubrics_metrics.name: Architecture / Structure
rubrics_metrics.description: Does the hour (or piece) have a structure, or is it a string of bits?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether the work as a whole has shape — beyond discrete jokes, is there an organizing architecture that ties material together.

rubrics_metrics.name: Risk
rubrics_metrics.description: Does the comic try anything that could fail?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ask whether anything was attempted that could have failed; risk signals creative ambition even when execution is uneven.

rubrics_metrics.name: Earned weight
rubrics_metrics.description: If the special or episode turns serious, has it earned the right?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether tonal shifts pay off — 'earned weight' means emotional or serious moments are justified by preceding material and do not feel tacked on.

rubrics_metrics.name: Originality
rubrics_metrics.description: Are the premises ones we've heard before, or new?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish between novel premises and familiar premises merely performed well; originality concerns both idea-level novelty and fresh execution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Resonance
rubrics_metrics.description: Does the special (or piece) sit with you the next day?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider whether the work lingers — 'are you still thinking about it tomorrow?' — as a measure of lasting impact beyond immediate laughs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Character consistency (sitcom)
rubrics_metrics.description: Do characters act and speak in ways consistent with who they are established to be?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For sitcom episodes, check that characters remain consistent across beats; inconsistency can undermine jokes and emotional turns.

rubrics_metrics.name: A-story / B-story interweaving (sitcom)
rubrics_metrics.description: Are the episode's main (A) and secondary (B) storylines effectively interwoven?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate how well multiple storylines balance and support each other to create a satisfying half-hour.

rubrics_metrics.name: Joke density per page (sitcom/scripted TV)
rubrics_metrics.description: Is the number of jokes per script page appropriate to the form?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For sitcom episodes, consider 'joke density per page' as a script-level analogue to laughs-per-minute in stand-up; measures pacing and comedic efficiency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Emotional turn that justifies the half-hour (sitcom)
rubrics_metrics.description: Is there an emotional shift or turn that justifies the episode's runtime?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether an emotional or thematic payoff validates the episode's shape and length, not merely a procession of jokes.

rubrics_metrics.name: World-building economy (sitcom)
rubrics_metrics.description: Does the episode build its world efficiently without exposition for its own sake?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoidance of gratuitous exposition; world-building should serve jokes or character and be economical.

rubrics_metrics.name: Surprise within form (sitcom)
rubrics_metrics.description: Does the episode deliver surprises while still operating within its formal boundaries?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for unexpected turns or inventive uses of the sitcom form that don't betray genre expectations but still surprise.

rubrics_metrics.name: One clear comedic engine (sketch)
rubrics_metrics.description: Does the sketch have one clear central comedic idea or engine?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sketches should center on a single strong premise that drives the humor; clarity of the engine prevents diffuse jokes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Escalation, not repetition (sketch)
rubrics_metrics.description: Does the sketch escalate the premise rather than simply repeat it?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer progressive escalation of stakes or absurdity over rote repetition; escalation keeps momentum and payoff.

rubrics_metrics.name: Strong button (sketch)
rubrics_metrics.description: Does the sketch end on a strong 'button' (a punchy final gag)?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A strong closing gag or 'button' anchors the sketch and gives the audience a satisfying endpoint.

rubrics_metrics.name: Performances elevate the writing (sketch)
rubrics_metrics.description: Do performances elevate the writing (or does the writing elevate the performances)?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess interplay of performance and script; strong performances can lift mediocre writing and vice versa, but both should ideally reinforce each other.

rubrics_metrics.name: Don't praise difficulty for its own sake (critic's trap)
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid giving credit solely because something was hard to do.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critics should not praise difficulty independent of execution or impact; difficulty is not a proxy for quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Don't conflate intent with execution (critic's trap)
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not assume good intentions equal good results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate what appears on the stage/screen rather than the performer's stated aims; assess execution separately from intent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Don't review the comic instead of the work (critic's trap)
rubrics_metrics.description: Focus criticism on the work itself rather than on the comic's personality or biography.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid turning reviews into profiles or moral judgments about the performer when the task is to evaluate the piece presented.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acknowledge laughter as data even when craft is uneven (critic's trap)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use audience laughter as evidence even if the craft appears inconsistent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that laughter is a form of empirical data about what works; note where audience response diverges from perceived craft quality.
